entries.title: How the Blackhawks plan to improve their defense without changing their systems
entries.summary: <p>After a team-wide reckoning Saturday night through Monday morning, the <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/blackhawks" target="_blank" >Blackhawks</a> elected not to overhaul their systems — or even make any major tweaks — but to instead bear down on numerous points of emphasis within those systems.</p><p>At practice Monday, they spent the first half working on defensive-zone coverage. Then they stopped for a rare mid-practice meeting before returning to the ice to work on tracking in transition.</p><p>Considering how inept the Hawks have looked at times this season — including throughout their 9-2 drubbing Saturday that prompted this reality check — fans may be confused why they wouldn't burn everything and start from scratch.</p><p>But coach Jeff Blashill, whose job security was <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/blackhawks/2026/11/08/blackhawks-jeff-blashill-no-coaching-changes-adjustments" >reiterated</a> by team sources Sunday, believes a rash decision like that wouldn't pay off Thursday against the Sabres.</p><p>"If you make full-scale changes to what you do, you could walk on the ice Thursday and guys [could] be super hesitant and not know what they’re doing," Blashill said. "And that’s the worst possible situation."</p><p>Blashill added players indicated "full belief in the systems" during team meetings Sunday. Everyone understands the Hawks need to allow fewer scoring chances than they have so far, though.</p><p>Natural Stat Trick's public model has the Hawks giving up the second-most chances (30.3) — per 60 minutes of five-on-five play — in the NHL. Blashill has been mocked plenty for the Hawks' internal stats, but they paint a comparable picture.</p><p>"Just [as] a big blanket statement, we've got to give up less chances," Blashill said. "The early part of the year, we didn't create much and we gave up a lot. As the year went along, we started creating more but we still gave up too many."</p><p>Blashill later said the Hawks have allowed the most two-on-one rushes in the league "by a lot," which certainly matches with the eye test.</p><p>Many of those rushes are enabled by players making mistakes within the Hawks' <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/blackhawks/2026/10/16/blackhawks-forward-lineup-strategy-forechecking-puck-pressure" >aggressive 2-1-2 forecheck</a>, which Blashill admitted he would love to one day resemble the Hurricanes' renowned relentless approach.</p><p>Within that system, defensemen are encouraged to step up along the walls in the neutral zone, but the Hawks emphasized Monday they need to pick and choose when to do that instead of doing it automatically every time.</p><p>"On strong-side plays and on goalie-touch plays, [they need to] be way more cautious and aware of whether the 'F3' is there or not," Blashill said.</p><p>The F3s (high forwards) need to be more responsible, too. In particular, they need to stick to the middle of the ice instead of veering toward the wall. If they veer and the near defenseman steps up, that creates a situation primed for a two-on-one rush against.</p><p>"We want to be a pressure team, but you can’t chase pressure," Blashill said. "Sometimes you have to read those situations and live another day."</p><div class="Enhancement" data-align-center><div class="Enhancement-item"> <div class="ExternalContent-wrapper" > <div class="TweetUrl"> <blockquote class="twitter-tweet"><p lang="en" dir="ltr">An example of how not to forecheck from Saturday: Blackhawks have no F3 yet D Ian Cole steps up in the neutral zone anyway, leading to a 2-on-1 goal against <a href="https://t.co/q95ZZrD1ZF">pic.twitter.com/q95ZZrD1ZF</a></p>— Ben Pope’s Video Clips (@BenPopeCSTclips) <a href="https://x.com/BenPopeCSTclips/status/2119942836326125844?ref_src=twsrc%5Etfw">November 9, 2026</a></blockquote> <script async src="https://platform.x.com/widgets.js" charset="utf-8"></script> </div> </div> </div></div><p>Decision-making by defensemen within the defensive zone was another focus area Monday — in addition to basic defensive fundamentals like going "stick-on puck, body-on-body" and staying on the goal side of opponents.</p><p>The Hawks encourage defensemen to jump out from the net-front toward the boards if they can kill a play by doing so, but they need to rein in how often that happens.</p><p>"[The message was], 'Strike when you can in the 'D'-zone, but get to your post,'" defenseman Wyatt Kaiser said. "We [need to] be a little more cerebral, not just hanging on guys. Get to them, get back. If you can't get to them, let the center get to them. We don't need to be spreading out."</p><p>Blashill said the defensemen need to do "a better job of owning both posts," which involves "not getting tied up" with box-outs or going to the wrong post altogether.</p><p>It's worth noting the league's stoutest five-on-five defensive team (the Panthers) still allow 21.8 scoring chances per 60 minutes per Natural Stat Trick — only about 30% fewer than the Hawks do.</p><p>The margins are relatively slim in the NHL. That's why the Hawks believe a handful of fewer mistakes per game could actually make a big difference.</p><p>"Are you going to see a drastic difference next game? It's probably not going to look that different, to be honest," Kaiser said. "Maybe we win a few more battles, or [we] get a few blocked shots, or a few more shots come in and the 'D' are there and nothing happens.</p><p>"We're going to do what we do and do it a little bit better."</p>
entries.author: Ben Pope

entries.title: Blackhawks' problems start with GM Kyle Davidson
entries.summary: <p>Here’s the thing about rebuilds: They can keep people employed who shouldn’t be.</p><p>We’ve seen it from every team in town. Now we have the <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/blackhawks" >Blackhawks,</a> who are in Year 5 of a rebuild that has gone off course.</p><p>After making strides last season, then raising expectations this season, the Hawks (4-13-1) entered Monday with the second-fewest points in the NHL — nine in 18 games. How bad is that? They’re on pace for 42 points, which would be their fewest in a full season since they totaled 31 in 1953-54, when a full season was 70 games.</p><p>So, yeah, things are bad, and it sure felt like the Hawks hit rock bottom Saturday night when the Stanley Cup champion Hurricanes pummeled them in a 9-2 game that wasn’t as close as the score indicates. That loss capped a horrendous 0-3 trip that had observers thinking significant changes could be coming. The Hawks were in crisis, and the coach’s seat appeared to be burning.</p><p>But when they practiced Monday, the general manager was not present.</p><p>Kyle Davidson began serving as interim GM in October 2021 after Stan Bowman resigned in the wake of the investigation into sexual-assault allegations against former video coach Brad Aldrich. The Hawks removed Davidson’s interim tag in March 2022 and have given him carte blanche to rebuild the team as he sees fit.</p><p>“There are some things that we need to fix that are going to take time,” Davidson said then. “Whether it’s three, five years, I don’t have an answer for that now. But we have to do this the right way.”</p><p>Well, three years came and went, and five years are now staring at Hawks fans, who are paying a tidy sum to watch bad hockey. So how does eight or 10 years sound? Because at this rate, the team won’t be rebuilt anytime soon, even with star center Connor Bedard around.</p><p>Davidson should’ve addressed all that and more Monday. Instead, he’ll speak to the media — and fans — Wednesday.</p><p>He’s in Toronto for GM meetings. His home is on fire, but he’ll put out the blaze in a couple of days. Would a Zoom call have killed him?</p><p>Coach Jeff Blashill was left to face the music again. Many thought his job was in peril — it still might be — but there he was Monday, leading practice and blowing the whistle to stop drills that had gone awry.</p><p>“Can’t have it!” he bellowed at one point.</p><p>Blashill, who coached mostly bad Red Wings teams from 2015 to 2022, is in a tough spot again. Like in Detroit, he doesn’t have everything he needs here, but he also isn’t getting enough from what he has.</p><p>He’s empathetic to the fans’ plight in all of this.</p><p>“I get the disappointment — our record is what our record is,” he said. “It’s not nearly where the fans thought it would be and not where we want it to be. We’re going to do everything we can to try to grind our way through this, get incrementally better, find our way to wins and, if we can do that, the satisfaction you get is awesome.</p><p>“That’s the only thing I could really say to [fans]. I can promise them whatever I want. That’s pretty much all bull---. We’re trying to grind like crazy to get better results through great process.”</p><p>The process that should be addressed is the one that procures players. Davidson went all in with the teardown, but he hasn’t done the same with the build-up. Yes, he acquired defenseman Bowen Byram and brought back Patrick Kane. But he didn’t do nearly enough to supplement all of his precious prospects with capable veterans. He could have addressed that Monday.</p><p>The biggest statement Davidson made in absentia was shipping out backup goalie Arvid Soderblom and calling up Drew Commesso. That’ll get the fans excited for the next home game Thursday, when the boo birds will fly at the first sight of folly. Davidson could’ve tried appealing to fans Monday, too.</p><p>And look who’s coming to town. It’s the Sabres, who went 14 years without a playoff berth before earning one last season. How many rebuilds is that? Do you remember the last time the Hawks went 14 seasons without making the playoffs? Of course you don’t, because it hasn’t happened — yet.</p><p>Davidson got lucky with Bedard as the No. 1 overall pick in 2023. Did he get unlucky or miscalculate by drafting Artyom Levshunov at No. 2 over Ivan Demidov in 2024? The jury is still out on Anton Frondell, the No.  3 pick in 2025. Meanwhile, other rebuilding teams are passing the Hawks left and right. Davidson could’ve talked about that, too.</p><p>Instead, we wait ’til Wednesday for Davidson to support the . . . let’s see . . . one, two, three . . . fourth coach he has hired.</p><p>When the popular perception is that the coach is the problem, it’s not a great look if the person who hired him isn’t there. If Davidson is spread too thin, maybe a director of hockey operations is necessary.</p><p>That way, someone would be there to put out the fire.</p>

entries.title: First day of practice: Is a new basketball powerhouse under construction at St. Laurence?
entries.summary: <p>St. Laurence’s campus has been under construction for a few years now, and a fieldhouse is going up next to the parking lot. That’s rare for a private school and a sign things are on the rise in Burbank.</p><p>If things go as planned on the basketball court this winter, St. Laurence might evolve from the most misspelled local high school into a new basketball powerhouse in the area.</p><p>Monday was the first day of practice across the state, and Roshawn Russell, who coached first-round NBA Draft pick Morez Johnson during his first three years at St. Rita, wore a wide smile as he discussed his current team. Russell is in his third year at St. Laurence and has one of the deepest, most talented squads in the state.</p><p>‘‘I love our group,’’ Russell said. ‘‘They have been together for a while and are very close. Ups and downs are expected, but they will be able to handle any adversity. This may be the deepest team I’ve had, one through 15. I’m confident in putting anyone in the game.’’</p><p>Senior Markese Peoples, a 6-2 guard who recently switched his college commitment from Central Michigan to UIC, is one of only six Division I seniors in the area.</p><p>‘‘Markese is unguardable,’’ Russell said. “He’s a leader and a great person, and his teammates love him. We will go as he goes. He knows that. He is the senior that will be on the floor the most, and we will follow his lead.’’</p><p>Peoples is rugged and physical, able to bully his way into the paint to score and rebound. He averaged 17 points and seven rebounds last season, but he took his game to a new level during the summer.</p><p>‘‘I’m stronger than most guards but able to do guard things,’’ Peoples said. ‘‘It is fun battling down low.’’</p><p>Peoples went under the radar last season but is considered one of the top players in the area and had his choice of several colleges.</p><p>‘‘Everything fell into place in a short period of time,’’ he said. “I love everything around [St. Laurence]. It changed my life, really. I’m forever thankful for what St. Laurence gave me.’’</p><div class="Enhancement" data-align-center> <div class="Enhancement-item" data-crop=""> <figure class="Figure"><a class="AnchorLink" id="image-250000" name="image-250000"></a> <picture data-crop="medium"> <source type="image/webp" width="490" height="275" data-srcset="https://cst.brightspotcdn.com/dims4/default/6ce06da/2147483647/strip/true/crop/5388x3024+0+284/resize/490x275!/format/webp/quality/90/?url=https%3A%2F%2Fchorus-production-cst-web.s3.us-east-1.amazonaws.com%2Fbrightspot%2Ffa%2Fb0%2F13ba2af5442f93742f60c4e6e746%2Fob-cst-111026-006.jpg 1x,https://cst.brightspotcdn.com/dims4/default/d82ea0c/2147483647/strip/true/crop/5388x3024+0+284/resize/980x550!/format/webp/quality/90/?url=https%3A%2F%2Fchorus-production-cst-web.s3.us-east-1.amazonaws.com%2Fbrightspot%2Ffa%2Fb0%2F13ba2af5442f93742f60c4e6e746%2Fob-cst-111026-006.jpg 2x" data-lazy-load="true" srcset="data:image/svg+xml;base64,PHN2ZyB4bWxucz0iaHR0cDovL3d3dy53My5vcmcvMjAwMC9zdmciIHZlcnNpb249IjEuMSIgaGVpZ2h0PSIyNzVweCIgd2lkdGg9IjQ5MHB4Ij48L3N2Zz4=" /> <source width="490" height="275" data-srcset="https://cst.brightspotcdn.com/dims4/default/1ca461d/2147483647/strip/true/crop/5388x3024+0+284/resize/490x275!/quality/90/?url=https%3A%2F%2Fchorus-production-cst-web.s3.us-east-1.amazonaws.com%2Fbrightspot%2Ffa%2Fb0%2F13ba2af5442f93742f60c4e6e746%2Fob-cst-111026-006.jpg" data-lazy-load="true" srcset="data:image/svg+xml;base64,PHN2ZyB4bWxucz0iaHR0cDovL3d3dy53My5vcmcvMjAwMC9zdmciIHZlcnNpb249IjEuMSIgaGVpZ2h0PSIyNzVweCIgd2lkdGg9IjQ5MHB4Ij48L3N2Zz4=" /> <img class="Image" alt="St. Laurence coach Roshawn Russell coaches Noah Corro (5), Markese Peoples (23) and Jeremiah Toney (4) on the first day of basketball practice. " srcset="https://cst.brightspotcdn.com/dims4/default/1ca461d/2147483647/strip/true/crop/5388x3024+0+284/resize/490x275!/quality/90/?url=https%3A%2F%2Fchorus-production-cst-web.s3.us-east-1.amazonaws.com%2Fbrightspot%2Ffa%2Fb0%2F13ba2af5442f93742f60c4e6e746%2Fob-cst-111026-006.jpg 1x,https://cst.brightspotcdn.com/dims4/default/68e60f2/2147483647/strip/true/crop/5388x3024+0+284/resize/980x550!/quality/90/?url=https%3A%2F%2Fchorus-production-cst-web.s3.us-east-1.amazonaws.com%2Fbrightspot%2Ffa%2Fb0%2F13ba2af5442f93742f60c4e6e746%2Fob-cst-111026-006.jpg 2x" width="490" height="275" data-src="https://cst.brightspotcdn.com/dims4/default/1ca461d/2147483647/strip/true/crop/5388x3024+0+284/resize/490x275!/quality/90/?url=https%3A%2F%2Fchorus-production-cst-web.s3.us-east-1.amazonaws.com%2Fbrightspot%2Ffa%2Fb0%2F13ba2af5442f93742f60c4e6e746%2Fob-cst-111026-006.jpg" data-lazy-load="true" src="data:image/svg+xml;base64,PHN2ZyB4bWxucz0iaHR0cDovL3d3dy53My5vcmcvMjAwMC9zdmciIHZlcnNpb249IjEuMSIgaGVpZ2h0PSIyNzVweCIgd2lkdGg9IjQ5MHB4Ij48L3N2Zz4=" > </picture> <div class="Figure-content"><figcaption class="Figure-caption"><p>St. Laurence coach Roshawn Russell coaches Noah Corro (5), Markese Peoples (23) and Jeremiah Toney (4) on the first day of basketball practice.</p></figcaption><span class="line"></span><div class="Figure-credit"><p>Kirsten Stickney/For the Sun-Times</p></div></div> </figure> </div> </div><p>Three experienced juniors also return: 6-6 Logan Brown, 6-4 Jeremiah Toney and 6-2 Noah Corro. Sophomores Evan Lemons and Lawrence Burnett will be major contributors, and Russell also expects 6-5 freshman Bennett Meier and 6-0 freshman Dakarai Simmons to pitch in.</p><p>‘‘Logan is a lot stronger, and his confidence level has risen,’’ Russell said. ‘‘He’s been a three-sport athlete all his life, Now he’s locked in on basketball, and the hard work is paying off.’’</p><p>Lemons is long and athletic and might be one of the breakout sophomores in the state.</p><p>The Vikings will need substantial contributions from the young stars because their schedule is extremely challenging. They open the season at the prestigious Tournament of Champions in Washington, play in all the top local events and will travel to Las Vegas for the Tarkanian Classic.</p><p>‘‘Nowadays, it is really difficult for a high-school kid to get college opportunities,’’ Russell said. ‘‘We have big goals and want to accomplish a lot this year, but my No. 1 will always be helping kids get to college. We have to play in some very competitive tournaments for these guys to be seen.’’</p><p>If Peoples lives up to his promise this winter and the young players around him continue to mature, anything is possible for St. Laurence.</p><p>‘‘I am hearing about the basketball team every day,’’ Toney said. ‘‘The school is definitely excited about the season.’’</p>

entries.title: Bridgeport neighbors raise concerns about police driving and scooter traffic after fatal crash
entries.summary: <p>A 39-year-old man riding a stand-up electric scooter was <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/crime/2026/11/05/electric-scooter-driver-dead-after-collision-with-cpd-vehicle-in-bridgeport" target="_blank" >killed last Thursday</a> after colliding with a marked Chicago police vehicle in Bridgeport, prompting nearby residents to raise concerns about driving habits and traffic safety in the neighborhood.</p><p>The victim, identified Monday as Bridgeport resident Hao Lin by the Cook County Medical Examiner’s Office, lived in the 3200 block of South Wallace Street. He was pronounced dead at 1:15 a.m. at Stroger Hospital , according to Chicago police.</p><p>According to Chicago police, officers were northbound on Princeton Avenue in a marked police vehicle while on patrol when their vehicle collided with the electric scooter operated by Lin.</p><p>Lin was treated at the scene by Chicago Fire Department personnel before being transported to Stroger, police said. The results of Lin's autopsy remain inconclusive, according to the medical examiner's office.</p><p>Both officers inside the police vehicle were transported to University of Illinois Hospital for treatment.</p><p>The circumstances surrounding the crash remain under investigation by CPD's Major Accidents Investigation Unit, so it's not yet known whether the officers or Lin are at fault. And Bridgeport residents interviewed said they see both police and scooter riders driving unsafely in the area.</p><p>Sira Rivera, a Bridgeport resident of more than five years who lives less than four blocks from the crash scene. He didn't see the crash but said he wasn't completely surprised it involved a police vehicle.</p><p>“The cops always run the stop signs in the neighborhood,” Rivera said. “They drive kind of crazy all the time.”</p><p>Other residents pointed to dangerous behavior among electric scooter and bicycle riders, saying they frequently ignore stop signs and traffic signals, creating risks for themselves and others.</p><p>Frank, a lifelong Bridgeport resident who declined to provide his last name, lives about a block from the crash scene. He said he’s noticed a pattern of scooter and bicycle riders disregarding traffic signals.</p><p>“A lot of scooter people just run right through the stop signs, the stoplights,” he said. </p><p>Concerns about scooter safety in Chicago come amid <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/crime/2026/11/06/electric-scooter-driver-67-killed-in-c" target="_blank" >another fatal crash involving an electric scooter last week.</a> The day after Lin's death, a 67-year-old man riding a stand-up electric scooter was killed in North Park after being struck by a speeding SUV.</p><p>Frank said riders who fail to stop at intersections put themselves at risk, particularly when vehicles approach at higher speeds.</p><p>He said scooter and bicycle riders should follow the same traffic rules as motorists.</p><p></p><p>“If everyone just sits there and abides by the laws of stopping at the stop signs or stoplights, I think it will go down a whole lot,” he added.</p>
entries.author: Christiana Freitag

entries.title: Mayor Johnson upends gunshot-detection pilot after voters resoundingly back the technology
entries.summary: <p>The 72% support in an advisory referendum for bringing gunshot-detection technology back to the streets of Chicago has apparently prompted Mayor Brandon Johnson to change his crime-fighting strategy.</p><p>Chief Procurement Officer Sharla Roberts disclosed the surprise about-face Monday while on the hot seat at a City Council budget hearing.</p><p>Roberts said her office initially planned a pilot program with one vendor that wasn't involved in a lengthy, competitive bidding process for a gunshot-detection contract. But the Johnson administration has now decided to let all of the “short-listed” bidders showcase their violence prevention strategies in the pilot, Roberts said.</p><p>The mystery program will still test a variety of ideas, including more violence intervention, “drone-based situational awareness, license plate recognition and incident response systems for evidence preservation.”</p><p>Gunshot-detection technology is still only part of the pilot.</p><p>Roberts acknowledged <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/elections/2026/11/04/shotspotter-advisory-referendum-gunshot-detection-technology-brandon-johnson-opposition" >voters’ support</a> for a technology her boss had scrapped prompted the administration to change course.</p><p>“The information from the referendum does play [into the mayor’s thinking] because … it spoke loudly. That’s what the community wants. So we are listening — not just to the alders. We’re listening to what the community wanted just as well,” Roberts said.</p><p>Input from police district personnel and a veiled warning from SoundThinking, the parent company of ShotSpotter, also contributed to Johnson's shift, Roberts said. The mayor got rid of ShotSpotter in 2024.</p><p>In an Oct. 27 letter, SoundThinking's attorney informed Roberts that, if the city was, in fact, planning to test crime-fighting strategies that included gunshot detection, ShotSpotter demanded to be part of it because the company was one of the “short-listed” firms.</p><p>A SoundThinking spokesperson said Johnson’s administration never contacted the company after its fall 2025 oral presentation and live-fire demonstration with the city. The spokesperson said the voters who backed the recent referendum on gunshot-detection technology "deserve to be heard, particularly in communities where gun violence is, unfortunately, a lived experience."</p><p>Far South Side Ald. Anthony Beale (9th), one of Johnson’s most outspoken Council critics, has accused the mayor of using the pilot as a stalling tactic to get past the mayoral election.</p><p>Beale likened the mayor’s change in strategy to playing Russian roulette with the lives of everyday Chicagoans.</p><p>“People are bleeding out in the street every single day because we don't have this technology, and we don't have time to play games with a hypothetical pilot program that we're making up in order to make it seem like we're doing something,” Beale told Roberts.</p><div class="Enhancement" data-align-center> about-face on gunshot detection technology.</p></figcaption><span class="line"></span><div class="Figure-credit"><p>LinkedIn</p></div></div> </figure> </div> </div><p>Downtown Ald. Brendan Reilly (42nd) reminded Roberts that Chicago has “gone more than two years without gunshot detection” and that <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/editorials/2025/02/18/shotspotter-mayor-johnson-gunshot-detection-police-technology-city-hall" >bids to replace the technology</a> formerly provided by ShotSpotter “came in 18 months ago.” Instead of choosing a replacement, Johnson announced a "no-bid pilot," Reilly said.</p><p>It’s been three years since Johnson honored a campaign promise to progressive supporters by <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/2024/02/13/mayor-johnson-to-end-shotspotter-deal-after-summer" >canceling the city’s contract</a> with ShotSpotter, which he derisively called a “walkie-talkie on a stick.”</p><p>Johnson and his progressive supporters viewed the technology as costly, ineffective and a contributor to overpolicing in Black and Brown communities, where the majority of gun violence occurs.</p><p>Afterward, the Council empowered then-Chicago Police Supt. Larry Snelling to <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/city-hall/2024/05/22/shotspotter-contract-wards-council-members-brandon-johnson-police-shootings-adam-toledo" >sign a new contract with ShotSpotter</a>. But Johnson declared the ordinance illegal, even after negotiating a costly extension to retain the technology through the 2024 Democratic National Convention in Chicago.</p><p>Johnson then launched an open competition to replace ShotSpotter. SoundThinking was one of 15 firms responding to a request for information and one of nine companies responding to a follow-up request for proposals.</p><p>Ald. Gilbert Villegas (36th) asked about the testing of gunshot-detection technologies during the bidding process — a process Roberts initially couldn't recall. She eventually characterized the tests as "demonstrations" in a controlled environment and said the pilot would allow for a better analysis.</p><p>Roberts was a no-show at another recent hearing. She infuriated Council members by sending a letter informing them the pilot program was about to begin in six police districts: Wentworth, Calumet, Englewood, Deering, Ogden and Harrison.</p><p>Against that backdrop, the nonbinding referendum garnered 72% support. On the day after the election, Johnson hinted strongly that he would not be moved by the overwhelming vote.</p><p>“I support technology, but it has to be technology that is credible. It has to be technology that’s actually effective. It has to be technology that safeguards our community from anything that could be detrimental to our privacy. So I’ve put forth a pilot," Johnson said then.</p><p>When Roberts first disclosed the mayor's change of heart, she had trouble explaining it, and Budget Chair Jason Ervin (28th) had difficulty understanding what she was trying to say.</p><p>“What’s that mean in English?” Ervin asked Roberts.</p><div class="RelatedList Enhancement" data-module data-align-center> <div class="RelatedList-title">Related</div> <ul class="RelatedList-items"> <li class="RelatedList-items-item"> <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/elections/2026/11/04/shotspotter-advisory-referendum-gunshot-detection-technology-brandon-johnson-opposition" >Most Chicago voters said they want ShotSpotter back, but that’s unlikely to sway Mayor Johnson</a> </li> <li class="RelatedList-items-item"> <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/2024/02/13/mayor-johnson-to-end-shotspotter-deal-after-summer" >Mayor Johnson to end ShotSpotter deal after summer, making good on key campaign promise</a> </li> <li class="RelatedList-items-item"> <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/editorials/2025/02/18/shotspotter-mayor-johnson-gunshot-detection-police-technology-city-hall" >Will search for new gunshot detection system lead back to ShotSpotter?</a> </li> </ul> </div> <p></p>

entries.title: Got a Thanksgiving holiday travel hack? We want to hear from you
entries.summary: <p>Thanksgiving is the busiest travel period of the year. </p><p>Last year, U.S. airports recorded their <a class="Link" href="https://www.reuters.com/world/us/us-screened-record-313-million-airline-passengers-sunday-2025-12-01/" target="_blank" >busiest day ever</a> (on the Sunday after Thanksgiving). Amtrak <a class="Link" href="https://media.amtrak.com/2026/11/amtrak-encourages-travelers-to-book-thanksgiving-travel-early-amid-historic-demand/" target="_blank" >handled</a> its largest passengers volume ever. And more people are <a class="Link" href="https://newsroom.aaa.com/2025/11/aaa-thanksgiving-travel-forecast-2025/" target="_blank" >traveling by car</a> than before the COVID-19 pandemic.</p><p>With congestion worse than ever, the Chicago Sun-Times wants to hear your hacks for traveling during Thanksgiving. We're looking for tips for flying, driving or taking a train.</p><p>Please fill out the form below oremail us at dstruett@suntimes.com.</p><p>We plan to publish some of them in the near future.</p><div class="Enhancement" data-align-center> <div class="HtmlModule"><a class="AnchorLink" id="html-embed-module-cc0000" name="html-embed-module-cc0000"></a><div class="contribly-contribute-v2" data-client="b20193c8-5c0c-4a5b-a770-64305c544c4e" data-assignment="e4e6ae70-ebb2-4fc3-81e3-5b8f7f0d83ce" data-display="inline" data-language="en-gb"></div><script type="text/javascript" src="https://s3-eu-west-1.amazonaws.com/contribly-widgets/contribute/contribute-v2.5.js"></script> </div> </div><p></p>
